bodyContents.0: This is the start of my weekly blogs. Though "Dev Logs" are the more correct term for them, as I intend to update this alongside my Portfolio. While my Portfolio page is more for finished pieces, this blog is more for the lines of "What did I do this week as a solo Game Designer?" This will be updated (hopefully) weekly to help get into a nice rhythm and also show off the smaller details of what's being made!
bodyContents.1: That said, this first post will be a blanket update of what I've been working on since August of 2025 all the way until the beginning of February. Videos and images of what has been made will be provided in the carousel above. Let's jump right into the meat and potatoes. I'll go in order of the months for an easier timeline.
bodyContents.2: August was the more foundation building for a personal project that I've been wanting to build for quite some time. This was mainly laying down the pavement for future planning. I created many documents in a Google Drive that started with just the "World Idea Info" - the sole World Building document. This then overflowed into a sub-doc of "Characters" - NPCs, Companions, Enemies, etc. The document that houses all written character creation. After that, I had to broaden my thought process. Since I already had a GDD template of ideas, it was when I realised it would be better to create a Feature Request document. Thus this was the month of working on it. Inside, I broke everything down into "Needs", "Wants", and "Desires" - or another way I've heard it being called the "ABCs" for mechanics. Listing every mechanic into the categories, the general idea of how I wanted the mechanic to look, and also making sure that Dependencies were written down as well. In total, there is about 20 pages worth of mechanics written in there, with some added in the later months. This document I always come back to. I will not share these on terms of privacy but also this is an idea that has been a dream of mine to make for a few years now. This month was also when I created the Azure Repository for the project I dubbed "Project Cogwheel".
bodyContents.3: September was the continuation of documentation regarding World Building. This was mostly slotting everything into place that would work alongside the Feature Request document. However, this month was more fitting to say that I created the private Jira board to finally be able to slot everything in place. Knowing how to work Jira and create tickets, I also learned how to create the workflow revolving the tickets, as well as making each Feature a ticket to hold all info in. That way, if I started to create Prototypes, I would be able to fit everything in. September was also the month where I created the first Prototype, which revolved around 3 of the "Need" mechanics. The first Prototype was started on Unreal Engine 5, version 5.6. The idea being a short Relay Race game that featured Multiplayer, Team Turn-Based, and the movement being based on a Dice Roll.
bodyContents.4: October and November were focused solely on what I dubbed the "TurnBasedProto" or "Proto 1". I had major hurdles to leap over, as this was the first in a while that I got back into Blueprinting and developing more than designing. There were many days of frustration from being stuck or having to fix a bug that I knew what the issue was, but not how to fix the issue. It also didn't help that I started with some of the biggest mechanics I knew nothing about: Multiplayer. There were also many days of research around the mechanic, and with an even bigger struggle since this Prototype was Top Down. Despite the struggle, parts of the prototype were a success. The Turn-Based parts of it, as well as the movement with the Dice Roll. I will add a video of what the "final look" of the prototype looks like. Unfortunately I stopped working on this around mid-November and dubbed this prototype a failure, and then reflected on why it failed and how I can do better with the next prototype. Even if I stopped working on Proto 1, I didn't stop working on other things. I created multiple level ideas. These were all created on draw.io. However, these are in the process of being moved to Miro to have a better structure and easier to link my notes to the layout.
bodyContents.5: December was a mixture of different parts, but also a break for the holidays. This was the starting month for the second prototype that I started to work on (and continue to work on to this day). I created "Proto 2" or what the project is called: "InteractionProto". This is focusing on different "Need" mechanics, which is an Inventory System, Equipment System, Player Interaction System and starting to create Item Data that the same setup can be used on later projects. This prototype I've been more confident in, and created a small level around the concept of what I wanted this to become. I've learned a lot from this prototype in different ways to do things, but also just getting better at being able to blueprint.
bodyContents.6: January was a continuation of working on the "InteractionProto", being able to mostly finish off the Inventory System. Inside the system, I learned how to allow players to drag and drop, have the inventory save what items and where they are placed inside the inventory, whether it being opened or closed, and being able to drag the item outside of the inventory to have the item drop. Additionally, the interaction with an item, as well as highlighting an item when the player is within a certain range.
bodyContents.7: The start of February - up until the 9th - was more rocky with the prototype, where adding the Equipment system somewhat broke the way that the drag and drop of items were working. Alongside this, I also started to work on modeling items that will be used in the prototype via Blender and learning how to do basic hand-drawn textures, just so that I know how the workflow is used. Within the carousel will be a video of the state of the prototype, as well as images of the models that have been made.

bodyContents.0: Last week was all about setting up the blog on this very website! Learning how to do this was interesting, but also frustrating. At first, I was going to do this just with HTML Bootstrap. However, I realized that this would not be a good way of setting this up. And so, I turned to JSON and Javascript with the help of Cursor.
bodyContents.1: By Friday, I was able to pretty much get everything set up and ready for the future posts! Hopefully I'll be able to keep up to date with these, as this will be beneficial to the journey ahead on what I'll be making and hopefully releasing.

bodyContents.0: Last week started with pushing the Dev Blog up to the server, along with some hotfixes since I tested the build out. Of course, testing while having it in developer mode is much different than when it's pushed to the public. I could only find so many bugs to fix before pushing. Luckily, there were no breaking bugs, and it was just placement that was an issue, so the hotfixes were quick.
bodyContents.1: After the hotfixes, I started to wrap up the migration from draw.io to Miro, which included all of my level bubble diagrams and level layouts. This was already halfway done, but there were still some that needed to be complete. Alongside this, I also worked on the more indepth bubble diagrams of the level I called "Fisher's Rest".
bodyContents.2: One key takeaway that I learned, is that if you ever start a level or a diagram, never EVER finish the diagram without writing down your notes. Looking at what I created before, and seeing that no notes were written down? It took me a bit of time to sort through my brain and ask myself "What the heck was I thinking of placing these symbols into this area? How do these symbols work in this area?" Suffice to say, there was a bit of adding, removing, and editing some of the symbols for "Fisher's Rest: Town Hall" in order to satisfy myself with what I wanted for my notes. Notes are everything when it comes to a level in progress!
bodyContents.3: The last thing worked on was my "InteractionProto", with two cases being worked on. First was adding the limitations to the Equipment Slots. At first, I added them without needing to solely state "Hey, only this certain category can be placed here!", mainly for testing purposes to see if they worked.At first, they did not. And so I had to go about fixing that. Once I was able to set things in there, I finally was able to add the category limitations. With a branch checking on the Event On Dragged Cancelled inside of the CoreSlot for if the item's category enum fit with the slot's enum (and some trial and error to fix a few issues while inputting the update), it finally started to work! You can now never put a Potion into the Head Slot! However, with new things comes new bugs.
bodyContents.4: The second case on "Proto 2" was trying to tie up some of the issues I found during the development of the equipment slots and the adding the Enum Check. One of the biggest issues was there being an error when an item was moved dragged into an Equipment Slot, or dragged back into an Inventory Slot. It was trial and error to figure out what was causing the issue. This issue came from the Inventory Slots having a certain array index that the Equipment Slots do NOT have. So with this, I had to add a check to see if it's less than 0 in order to skip an initial set for what the Inventory uses. This added yet another bug to the bug pile.
bodyContents.5: With the total of 5 bugs, and one being fixed, there are 4 bugs that I will be working on for the week of Feb 23rd. As for this post, I will also add some images of what was worked on for the level design, as well as a video of what was fixed.

bodyContents.0: Last week's focus was bug fixing, as well as solidifying a more Beta stepping stone for the main level inside of "InteractionProto". Bug fixing obviously came first. However, as you fix one issue, may more come into play. This was my issue, and most of them were introduced when adding the Equipment System on top of the Inventory System. Because the base that I created was geared more towards solely the Inventory System, adding the Equipment Slots was more or less breaking what was already working. Many of these issues are in separate parts of the system, which makes it worse since there is no "one fix all" solution. This was ultimately my lesson for this prototype. Always think about how the system will work as a whole, and not just the individual parts. This also opened my eyes to seeing that I have a long way to go when it comes to coding, that I know what I want out of a system but the output and implementation is the hardest part of a mechanic coming together.
bodyContents.1: Of course, I had to step back from bug fixing. I was getting no where except breaking it more as time went on over the week, and I was getting more and more frustrated with it. It's clear to me that I have a long ways of going when it comes to coding systems. For the time being, I will not show a video of the mechanic this time, because I practically broke it completely. I will post a video once I have it unbugged and working again. Continuing with the week, I still had Thursday and Friday ahead of me, and so I turned towards something that I always enjoy doing and absolutely love: Level Design. I thought "It's finally time for me to solidify the level and actually start to turn the layout into a 3D area, rather than just leaving it on paper." Level Design always makes me relaxed and focused, even from the first stages of planning. I will never tire of Level Design, knowing that I can create these areas or even worlds that a player will walk through? It's something that makes me smile while working.
bodyContents.2: Level Designing was during Thursday. I hunkered down and just worked through the day until I was finished with a good 3D layout that a player can go through without any hiccups, or too small of areas that the player cannot move through. I also was able to lay a foundation down as to where things will be placed, what items will be picked up, and how they will look within the level.
bodyContents.3: Friday was different, where I turned more towards doing some more modeling of items that will be in the level. I started with working on a bowl, which will hopefully turn into a bowl of beef stew. The bowl of course, was the easier part. It's the stew that will be the challenge. I started with trying to see if I could make the stew a 3D model, but after trial and error of it looking dead wrong to me, I decided to make a plane for where the texture of the stew will sit, and the last part I have to do is to create the texture. That will be next week, most likely as a wind down to bug fixing.

bodyContents.0: Last week doesn't have much of an update unfortunately. There was a lot more personal things going on, which took more priority. The time that I did have to work on anything was focused mostly on updating Jira and adding the bugs that I have found to actual tickets rather than just staying as comments inside of a blueprint. On top of that, I also updated tickets that were worked on based on what was worked on in the project. Knowing where I started and how far I've gotten, is eye opening. It's been a rocky road, but hopefully the road ahead won't be as bad. And also hopefully this week will be better, and that I can get more things done.

Time flew by as last week came and went. Suffice to say, I also wanted to throw Blender into a pit from the hours of work it said "Adios!" to on Friday. No backup, no quicksave, just the eternal darkness that my work went into. While working in the middle of fixing the UV on the Beef Stew model, and in the process of working on the base texture that would be used, Blender decided to completely remove all of my work on the texture, and revert some of the fixes on the UV. I almost wanted to quit then and there. However, I took a 10 minute break to calm down, then went back to working on it with a renewed vigor. I wasn't going to let Blender get the upper hand!
bodyContents.1: I've almost completely finished the bowl, and have about 15% to go. The rest of the UV (which is just a 4th of the side of the bowl left, that's already prepped to be finished up), and the texture. Before this, was more working on Jira to finally solidify everything. This included rewriting tickets to have a good layout and base to what should be written, as well as creating checklists. That way, everything is written out and not jumbled together, and I will be able to update the Jira more often to incorporate it more into my workflow rather than leaving it off to the side.

bodyContents.0: First things first, I scrapped the hand-made texture that I was fashioning for the bowl and soup. It hurt a little bit, but instead of using that time to make textures that are more difficult, I decided to use textures that are free to use and look more realistic. This also included using free stock images for parts of the soup texture as well. Of course, I couldn't find anything that had a semblance of what looked like beef stew, so I found something that still looks to what fit the theme of what I am creating, and found lentil soup. Once I found this, it took me a while to figure out how to turn it into a material that could be used. Normals, Roughness, and trying out some other parts like Displacement, I decided to just work with the normals and roughness to keep it easier on myself for whenever I wanted to use the model again. That way, I can reuse the bowl but change whatever is inside the bowl to what I desire.
bodyContents.1: Of course, there is always complications. When exporting into Unreal Engine, easily I noticed that there was something wrong with the model. It was a back and forth to try and fix it, but finally I was able to import it with no issues, minus the materials. I had to remake those inside of the engine, which was no issue at all since I had everything ready. And now, I have a reusable bowl model!
